passage:
Monday: A new girl, Preeti, joined Class 4B and took Jagdish's seat next to his best friend, Aman. Jagdish smiled very wide. "Welcome! You can have my seat forever!"
Wednesday: Jagdish carried Preeti's bag, gave her his whole tiffin, and followed her to the water tank, the library and the swings. "You're my favourite!" he told her loudly, glancing at Aman each time. At home he kicked his school shoes across the room.
Next Monday: Preeti asked to play with someone else. Jagdish's smile vanished. "Fine," he muttered, and sat alone at lunch. His teacher sat down beside him. "Missing Aman?" she asked. His chin wobbled.

qa.q: Whose seat did Preeti take on Monday?
qa.a: Jagdish's seat next to his best friend, Aman.

qa.q: Why does being extra sweet to Preeti feel right to Jagdish?
qa.a: The big kindness hides a jealousy he can't admit and keeps him close to Aman; kicking his shoes at home shows the anger underneath.

qa.q: What could the teacher do next to help Jagdish?
qa.a: Let him talk about missing Aman, then arrange a seat or game where Jagdish, Aman and Preeti can all be together.

qa.q: What might it be like for Preeti to be followed everywhere by Jagdish?
qa.a: She may feel crowded and a little confused, since his loud kindness doesn't feel quite real, which may be why she asked to play with someone else.

grounding: Over a week a boy who feels pushed aside by a new classmate becomes loudly, excessively friendly to her while his jealousy shows at home and at lunch.

subtype: Excessive kindness to a resented rival [Actor]
passage: Bhavna, you think your Nani was always sensible? Listen. When I was eight, a girl called Sushila joined our school in Nashik. On her first day, the teacher praised her handwriting, and mine had been the class favourite for two years. So what did I do? I became her shadow. I sharpened her pencils. I gave her my ribbons. I told everyone, "Sushila is my dearest friend in the whole world!" so often that the teacher said, "Minakshi, lower your voice." One evening my mother found me crying by the well and asked why. Only then did I say it: "Everyone likes her better." She hugged me and said feeling jealous didn't make me a bad girl. After that, I stopped performing. Sushila and I became real friends, slowly.

qa.q: What had been the class favourite for two years before Sushila arrived?
qa.a: Minakshi's handwriting, which the teacher had praised for two years.

qa.q: What was young Minakshi really feeling while she called Sushila her 'dearest friend'?
qa.a: She was jealous and afraid that everyone liked Sushila better; the loud friendliness covered a feeling she couldn't admit yet.

qa.q: What turning point helped Minakshi stop performing?
qa.a: Her mother finding her crying and asking why, then hugging her and saying that feeling jealous didn't make her a bad girl.

qa.q: How might Sushila have experienced Minakshi's shadowing?
qa.a: Sushila may have found the pencils and ribbons a bit much, and only felt a real friendship once Minakshi stopped performing.

grounding: A grandmother tells how, at eight, she hid jealousy of a praised new classmate behind loud, clinging friendliness until she could admit it.

subtype: Excessive kindness to a resented rival [Actor]
passage:
Rain delayed the school trip to the science museum, and forty children were squeezed into one bus. Kavitha had planned to sit with her best friend Rupa, as always. But Ayesha, the new girl already picked for the quiz team, got there first.
"Oh, Ayesha, you sit there!" Kavitha said, in a voice so sweet it sounded borrowed. All day she stuck beside Ayesha, offering chips, holding her umbrella, laughing loudly at every joke. When the teacher counted heads, Kavitha's arm was linked through Ayesha's.
On the ride back, when Ayesha dozed off, Kavitha stared at the rain and pinched the edge of her seat hard.
"Kavitha, are you okay?" Rupa whispered from behind.
"Of course!" Kavitha said, much too brightly.

qa.q: Where was the school trip going?
qa.a: To the science museum.

qa.q: What does Kavitha pinching the edge of her seat suggest she feels?
qa.a: She is upset and jealous that Ayesha took her place beside Rupa and on the quiz team, feelings her sweetness has been covering all day.

qa.q: What could Kavitha try when Rupa asks if she's okay?
qa.a: Admit one small true thing, like 'I missed sitting with you', which could let Rupa include her and ease the jealousy. 🙂

qa.q: How might Ayesha feel if she noticed Kavitha's voice 'sounded borrowed'?
qa.a: She might sense the kindness wasn't quite real and feel uneasy, even while being offered chips and an umbrella.

grounding: On a rainy school trip a girl who feels displaced by a new classmate sticks to her with sugary friendliness while hiding jealousy.

subtype: Excessive kindness to a resented rival [Actor]
passage:
When Miss Kulkarni gave the new girl, Lalremsiami, the narrator's part in the Class 4 play, Damini, who had been narrator last year, clapped the loudest.
After that, Damini was everywhere Lalremsiami went. She walked her to the water cooler. She lent her the new twenty-four colour pencils she never let anyone touch. "You're SO good at reading aloud! You're the best in the whole class!" she said, three times before lunch.
Lalremsiami smiled, a little puzzled. "Thanks... you don't have to wait for me."
"I WANT to!" Damini said, too loudly.
At home in their Pune flat that evening, Damini coloured a picture of the play stage. She pressed so hard on the crayon that it snapped, and she threw both halves in the bin. When Mummy asked about school, Damini said, "I have a new best friend," and didn't look up.

qa.q: What did Damini lend Lalremsiami?
qa.a: The new twenty-four colour pencils she never let anyone touch.

qa.q: Why might being extra sweet to Lalremsiami feel right to Damini?
qa.a: Damini seems hurt about losing the narrator's part, but being jealous feels wrong, so loud kindness hides it even from herself; the snapped crayon hints at what is underneath.

qa.q: What small step could Mummy take when Damini doesn't look up?
qa.a: Mummy could sit with Damini and ask about the play, perhaps saying it's okay to feel sad about not being narrator, so the hidden feeling can be named.

qa.q: What is it like for Lalremsiami to be followed everywhere and praised so much?
qa.a: Lalremsiami seems puzzled and a little crowded, grateful yet unsure why Damini won't let her walk alone, which makes settling in feel strange.

grounding: Shows a child displaced from the narrator's role by a new classmate becoming overly sweet and clingy, with jealousy leaking out only in the snapped crayon.

subtype: Excessive kindness to a resented rival [Actor]
passage:
"Ritu! Ritu, wait! I saved you a seat!"
"Oh, thanks, Kalyani. But I was going to sit with—"
"No, sit here, near me. Want my mango slice? You can have all of it."
"You gave me your eraser yesterday too."
"Because you're so nice! Everyone thinks so. Ma'am thinks so. Ma'am made you class monitor, right? After just two weeks! That's amazing. Amazing!"
"Um. You were monitor last term, weren't you?"
"Doesn't matter! Being monitor is boring anyway." Kalyani, ten, laughed a bit too high. "Come to the library with me after? And then the swings? I'll wait for you after class, okay?"
"Kalyani, are you... okay?"
"Of course I'm okay! Why wouldn't I be okay?"
Under the bench, she was tearing the edge of her tiffin paper into tiny strips.

qa.q: What did Kalyani offer Ritu to eat?
qa.a: Kalyani offered her mango slice: "You can have all of it."

qa.q: What does Kalyani tearing her tiffin paper into strips suggest about how she feels?
qa.a: It hints that under the loud praise she is upset, probably jealous about losing the monitor's job, a feeling she can't admit even to herself.

qa.q: How could an adult who noticed Kalyani's too-high laugh support her?
qa.a: By talking with Kalyani privately, saying it's normal to feel sad about not being monitor any more, and helping her find a real way to be friends with Ritu without pretending.

qa.q: Why might Ritu ask, "are you... okay?"
qa.a: Ritu seems to sense the praise is too much and too fast, and feels uneasy rather than welcomed, as if something doesn't fit.

grounding: Illustrates a child who feels displaced by a new classmate made monitor and responds with loud, clinging friendliness that covers jealousy.
